## What it is

Acoziborole is a single-dose oral treatment for human African trypanosomiasis caused by *Trypanosoma brucei gambiense*, given as three 320 mg tablets, and on 27 February 2026 the committee for medicines for human use (CHMP) of the European Medicines Agency adopted a positive scientific opinion for early- and advanced-stage disease in adults and in adolescents aged 12 years and older who weigh at least 40 kg (Drugs for Neglected Diseases initiative [DNDi], 2026). In the pivotal single-arm phase 2/3 trial, which enrolled 208 patients aged 15 years or older in the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Guinea, the 18-month success rate in late-stage disease was 95.2% (95% CI 91.2 to 97.7), while 14% of patients had drug-related adverse events, all mild or moderate, and four deaths were judged unrelated to treatment (Betu Kumeso et al., 2023).

## Why it matters

Zambia is relevant for a different reason, as the form of the disease found here is *T. b. rhodesiense*, which is endemic in 13 countries including Zambia, with 24 cases reported across four countries in 2023 (Wendt et al., 2025). A study covering the Eastern, Muchinga and Lusaka provinces identified 64 cases and concluded that the Zambian health system could not adequately handle them, with late or poor diagnosis attributed to a lack of qualified laboratory technicians and diagnostic equipment (Mwiinde et al., 2022). The CHMP opinion covers gambiense disease only (DNDi, 2026), although a laboratory study reported consistent activity of acoziborole against rhodesiense strains, including a multidrug-resistant field isolate, and its authors expect similar efficacy in patients, which clinical data have yet to confirm (Cal et al., 2026).

## What to remember

We should remember that a positive regulatory opinion is not a treatment guideline, as DNDi describes it as groundwork for approval in the Democratic Republic of the Congo and for a later revision of the WHO treatment guidelines (DNDi, 2026). For Zambian practice the immediate lesson lies in diagnosis, because a single-dose cure of any kind depends on cases being found early, and the rhodesiense evidence for acoziborole is still preclinical.
